title: Acts
intro: 40 days through the book of Acts, from Jerusalem to Rome, one verse at a time.

posts.caption: Acts continues the story after Jesus' resurrection. It is the sequel to Luke's Gospel, written by the same author, and both books are addressed to a man named Theophilus. Tradition holds the author was Luke, a doctor who traveled with Paul. It opens with the risen Jesus appearing to his followers over forty days. Starting today, 40 days through Acts, one verse at a time.

Jesus' last words to his followers before he is taken up, and a rough outline of the whole book. The story moves outward in widening circles: Jerusalem (chapters 1 to 7), Judea and Samaria (8 to 12), and then across the Roman world to Rome itself. Samaria lay between Judea and Galilee, home to a people many Jews of the time avoided.

The Ascension. Jesus is taken up into a cloud on the Mount of Olives, just east of Jerusalem, and two men in white speak to the stunned disciples. Luke describes two men in radiant clothing at the empty tomb, too (Luke 24:4). Many churches mark Ascension Day forty days after Easter.

Pentecost, Greek for "fiftieth," was the Jewish harvest festival of Shavuot, held fifty days after Passover, so Jerusalem was crowded with pilgrims. Visitors from many nations hear the disciples speaking in their own languages. In both Hebrew and Greek, the word for spirit also means wind or breath. Christians celebrate Pentecost fifty days after Easter.

Peter's first sermon ends with about three thousand people baptized, and Luke gives this snapshot of the new community. "Fellowship" is the Greek koinonia, meaning sharing or partnership; the next verses say they held their possessions in common and gave to anyone in need. Many readers see "the breaking of bread" as shared meals that included the Lord's Supper, or communion.

Peter and John are heading into the temple for afternoon prayer. A man who has been unable to walk since birth, carried to the gate every day to beg, asks them for money. Peter's reply has become one of the best-known lines in Acts. Acting "in the name of" Jesus means acting by his authority, a phrase that runs through these early chapters.

After the healing, Peter and John are arrested and questioned by the Sanhedrin, Jerusalem's ruling council of priests and elders. "Unschooled" translates a Greek word meaning "unlettered": they had no formal training in the law. These were fishermen from Galilee, and the council is struck by how boldly they speak.

posts.display: “Leave these men alone. Let them go! For if their purpose or endeavor is of human origin, it will fail. But if it is from God, you will not be able to stop them. You may even find yourselves fighting against God.”
posts.caption: The apostles are arrested again, and the council wants them put to death. Then Gamaliel, one of the most respected Jewish teachers of the day, stands up and gives this advice. Acts later says Paul had studied under him. The Mishnah, an early collection of Jewish teaching, remembers him with great honor.

As the community grows, Greek-speaking Jewish believers complain that their widows are being overlooked in the daily food distribution. The apostles ask the community to choose seven trusted men to take it on. Many churches see this as the origin of deacons, from the Greek diakonos, "servant." Two of the Seven, Stephen and Philip, take center stage next.

Stephen is put on trial and gives a long speech retelling Israel's history. It ends with him being dragged out of the city and stoned, the first Christian martyr, from the Greek martys, "witness." His last words echo Jesus' words on the cross in Luke's Gospel. Those stoning him lay their cloaks at the feet of a young man named Saul.

Persecution scatters the believers, and Philip, one of the Seven, preaches in Samaria. Then, on a desert road toward Gaza, he meets a royal treasurer from Ethiopia reading the prophet Isaiah in his chariot. "Ethiopia" here probably means the kingdom of Kush, in today's Sudan, where Candace was a title for the queen. Philip explains the passage, and the man is baptized by the roadside.

Saul, the young man who watched Stephen die, is heading to Damascus with authority to arrest followers of "the Way," an early name for the movement. A light from heaven flashes around him, and he falls to the ground. Notice the question: Jesus says Saul is persecuting him, not just his followers. Saul, better known as Paul, will become the central figure of the rest of Acts.

posts.display: “Brother Saul,” he said, “the Lord Jesus, who appeared to you on the road as you were coming here, has sent me so that you may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.”
posts.caption: Saul arrives in Damascus blind and goes three days without eating or drinking. A believer named Ananias is told in a vision to go to him, and he objects, knowing Saul's reputation. He goes anyway, and his first word is "Brother." In the next verse something like scales falls from Saul's eyes, the origin of the English phrase.

Peter is praying on a rooftop in Joppa, today's Jaffa, part of Tel Aviv. In a vision he sees a sheet lowered from heaven full of animals, including ones Jewish food laws called unclean, and he is told to eat. He refuses, and the voice answers with this, three times over. At that moment, messengers arrive from a Roman officer named Cornelius.

Cornelius is a Roman centurion who worships Israel's God but is not Jewish, and Peter admits that Jewish custom kept him from visiting a non-Jew's home. He goes anyway and realizes his vision was about people, not just food. While he is still speaking, the Holy Spirit comes on Cornelius's household. In Acts, this is when the message decisively reaches the Gentiles, meaning non-Jews.

Believers scattered by persecution reach Antioch, one of the great cities of the Roman Empire (today Antakya, in southern Turkey), and begin sharing the message with Greeks too. Barnabas, whose nickname means "Son of Encouragement," brings Saul to help teach. The name "Christian" appears only three times in the New Testament, and this is the first.

King Herod Agrippa I, a grandson of Herod the Great, has executed the apostle James and jailed Peter. An angel leads Peter out by night, and he goes to the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, where believers are praying for him. The servant girl Rhoda is so overjoyed she forgets to open the gate. John Mark is traditionally the author of Mark's Gospel.

From Antioch, Barnabas and Saul are sent off on what is often called Paul's first missionary journey, to Cyprus and then into today's Turkey. A few verses later Luke notes that Saul "was also called Paul." His name wasn't changed at his conversion: Saul was his Hebrew name and Paul (Paulus) his Roman one, and from here on the narrator calls him Paul.

In Lystra, in today's central Turkey, Paul heals a man who had never walked, and the crowd decides Barnabas and Paul are the gods Zeus and Hermes in human form. The priest of Zeus even brings bulls to sacrifice. The two insist they are only human. Speaking to people who didn't know the Jewish scriptures, they point to rain and harvests as signs of God's goodness.

One of the biggest debates of the early church: must non-Jewish believers be circumcised and keep the law of Moses? Jesus' first followers were all Jews, and circumcision was the ancient sign of God's covenant with Abraham, so to many it seemed essential. Leaders gather in Jerusalem, usually dated around AD 49, and Peter, remembering Cornelius, gives this answer.

James, whom Paul calls "the Lord's brother," a leader of the Jerusalem church, announces the decision: non-Jewish believers do not have to become Jews. They are asked only to avoid a few things, such as food offered to idols and eating blood. Many scholars see these as echoing rules in Leviticus for foreigners living among Israel. A letter goes out, and the church in Antioch rejoices.

Paul, now traveling with Silas and young Timothy, keeps finding his plans blocked until he reaches Troas, on the coast of today's Turkey. There he has this vision. Macedonia is in northern Greece, so this is Paul's first step into Europe. In the next verse the narrator switches from "they" to "we," and tradition reads these "we" passages as the author joining the journey.

In Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia, Paul finds women gathered to pray by the river on the Sabbath. Lydia, from Thyatira in today's Turkey, sells purple cloth, a luxury good often colored with costly dye. A "worshiper of God" was a non-Jew drawn to Israel's God. Lydia is often called the first recorded convert in Europe, and her home becomes the new church's base.

Paul frees a slave girl from a spirit used for fortune-telling, and her owners, angry at losing their income, have Paul and Silas beaten and jailed. At midnight, feet locked in the stocks, they are singing. An earthquake throws open the doors, and the jailer, about to take his own life, instead asks how to be saved and is baptized with his household that night.

Driven out of Thessalonica and Berea, Paul reaches Athens, the old center of Greek philosophy. He is invited to explain his ideas at the Areopagus, the name of a rocky hill near the Acropolis and of the council named after it. He begins with something he noticed walking around the city. Ancient Greek writers also mention altars to "unknown gods" in and around Athens.

Paul's speech in Athens quotes Greek poets, not the Hebrew scriptures. "We are His offspring" comes from Aratus, a poet from Paul's own home region of Cilicia, and the first line is often attributed to the poet Epimenides. When Paul mentions resurrection, some listeners scoff, but a few believe, including a council member and a woman named Damaris.

In Corinth, a busy Greek trading city, Paul makes tents with Priscilla and Aquila, a Jewish couple expelled from Rome by Emperor Claudius. Facing opposition, he receives this vision and stays a year and a half. An inscription found at Delphi dates the governor Gallio, mentioned a few verses later, to around AD 51, giving one of the firmest dates in Paul's life.

Paul spends more than two years in Ephesus, near today's Selçuk on Turkey's west coast, teaching daily in a lecture hall. The "province of Asia" was the Roman province in western Turkey, not the continent. His success hurt the trade in shrines of the goddess Artemis, whose temple there was one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World, and set off a riot.

On his way to Jerusalem, Paul stops at the port of Miletus and sends for the church leaders from Ephesus to say goodbye. Of Paul's major speeches in Acts, this is the only one given to fellow believers. "Finish my course" is a runner's image of completing a race, one Paul also uses in his letters.

Paul ends his farewell by reminding the leaders that he worked with his own hands to support himself and others. Then he quotes Jesus, and this saying appears in none of the four Gospels. It is one of the few sayings of Jesus recorded outside them. Afterward they all kneel to pray, weep, and walk him to his ship.

At Caesarea, a prophet named Agabus ties his own hands and feet with Paul's belt to show that Paul will be bound in Jerusalem. Paul's friends, the narrator among them, beg him not to go. This is his reply. Many readers see a parallel with Jesus in Luke's Gospel, who also set out for Jerusalem knowing what awaited him.

A crowd attacks Paul in the temple courts, and Roman soldiers take him into custody. About to be flogged for questioning, he mentions he is a Roman citizen, and everything stops, since Roman law protected citizens from such treatment. The commander's name, Claudius Lysias, suggests he bought his citizenship under Emperor Claudius, as new citizens often took the emperor's name.

Brought before the Sanhedrin, Paul splits the council by raising the resurrection, which Pharisees believed in and Sadducees rejected. That night, back in the Roman barracks, he has this vision. Soon more than forty men swear not to eat until they have killed him, but Paul's nephew hears of the plot, and Paul is moved to Caesarea with an escort of nearly five hundred soldiers.

In Caesarea, a Roman port on the coast of today's Israel, Paul is tried before the governor Felix. Later Felix and his wife Drusilla, a Jewish princess, listen to Paul privately, until the topics get uncomfortable. Felix hoped for a bribe and left Paul in prison for two years. The Roman historian Tacitus said Felix wielded a king's power with the mind of a slave.

Two years later, a new governor, Festus, proposes moving Paul's trial to Jerusalem, though his accusers had planned to ambush him on the way. Paul uses his right as a Roman citizen to appeal his case to the emperor himself. The "Caesar" at this time was Nero. Festus replies, "To Caesar you will go!"

Before he leaves for Rome, Paul speaks before King Herod Agrippa II, a great-grandson of Herod the Great, and tells his conversion story, the third account of it in Acts. The King James Version famously renders the king's reply, "Almost thou persuadest me to be a Christian." Paul's answer ends with a wry touch: "except for these chains."

Paul sails for Rome as a prisoner. Luke notes it was already "after the Fast," meaning Yom Kippur in the autumn, when sailing the Mediterranean grew dangerous. A violent northeaster drives the ship off course for days without sun or stars. Then Paul stands up and says an angel has promised that everyone on board will survive.

After two weeks adrift, the ship runs aground and breaks apart, but all 276 people on board reach shore alive. The island is Malta. When a viper fastens onto Paul's hand at the fire and he is unharmed, the islanders decide he must be a god. Malta still honors Paul, and St. Paul's Bay is traditionally where the ship came ashore.

After three months on Malta, Paul sails on to Italy. Believers from Rome come out to meet him at the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns, stops on the Appian Way, the great Roman road whose paving stones can still be walked today. Paul had written his letter to the Romans a few years earlier; now he finally meets them, though as a prisoner.

Acts ends with Paul under house arrest in Rome, still welcoming visitors and teaching. The very last word of the book in Greek is akolytos, "unhindered." Acts never says what happened to Paul next; early Christian tradition holds that he was executed in Rome under Nero. That's the book of Acts. Thank you for reading it with me.
